Cats FAQ

Discover answers to common questions about your feline friends.

Cats purr for many reasons — contentment, self-soothing, healing, and even communication. Kittens purr to signal their mothers they're content, while adult cats purr when they're happy or to calm themselves during stressful situations. The exact mechanism involves the laryngeal muscles vibrating at specific frequencies.

Indoor cats typically live 12 to 18 years, with some reaching their 20s. Outdoor cats generally have shorter lifespans due to exposure to predators, accidents, and disease. Proper nutrition, regular veterinary care, and a safe environment significantly extend a cat's lifespan.

Cats do see color, but not as vividly as humans. They see blues and greens well, but reds appear more greenish to them. Cats have around 200 degrees of visual range compared to humans' 180 degrees, giving them an excellent peripheral vision advantage for hunting.

Cats are champion sleepers, averaging 12 to 16 hours of sleep per day. This evolutionary trait stems from their hunting nature — they conserve energy for short bursts of activity. Senior cats often sleep even more, sometimes up to 20 hours daily.

Whiskers are sensory organs that help cats navigate their environment and measure spaces. They're extremely sensitive to changes in air currents, allowing cats to detect obstacles, changes in their surroundings, and even the mood of other animals. Cats have about 12 whiskers on each side of their face.

A twitching tail can indicate various emotions depending on the context. Slow twitches usually signal focus or mild interest, while rapid twitching or thrashing suggests irritation, excitement, or frustration. A tail held high generally indicates confidence and happiness, while a tucked tail signals fear or uncertainty.

Cats have an incredible righting reflex developed through their flexible spine and inner ear balance. Within milliseconds of falling, cats twist their spine to orient themselves and extend their limbs to land on their feet. This ability develops around 7 weeks of age and improves with practice throughout their lives.

While cats are often perceived as aloof, they form strong bonds with their owners and social groups. Cats show affection differently than dogs — through slow blinks, head bunts, and choosing to spend time near you. They do appreciate independence and personal space, which is part of their charm and unique personality.
